scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Explain what React re-renders, and why. Fix the key bug that moves typed text. And fix a counter stuck at one, a stale closure.

scenes.title: Why does the text move?
scenes.statement: A todo list renders each row with key equal to its index. Add one todo on top. The typed text stays in row one.

example.output: '2 litres' ends on the wrong row

scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, index keys, and a new todo added on top. We want to know why the text lands on Pay rent.

scenes.head: A host with a seating chart
scenes.say: Think of a host with a seating chart. Last night: Ann, Bo, Cy. Tonight Dee joins at the front. A bad host reseats everyone. A good host reads name tags. React is that host, and the key is the name tag.

scenes.head: Index keys, step by step
scenes.say: Before: Buy milk has key zero, Walk dog has key one. You type two litres into key zero. Now Pay rent is added on top, and takes key zero. React sees key zero again, so it reuses that row, typed text and all. Buy milk shifts to key one. Walk dog gets key two, a new row.

scenes.head: The fix is one word
scenes.say: Left: key is the index, so identity follows the position. Right: key is the id, so identity follows the todo. Buy milk keeps its id, and its typed text. Pay rent is simply a new row. Use a stable, unique id from your data.
Your turn. A developer sets key to Math dot random on every row. Each row has a controlled input, so it re-renders on every keystroke. What happens as you type? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `key={Math.random()}` on rows. What happens when you type?

scenes.head: What React does with a key
scenes.say: Remount. A new key is a new item, so the text is gone. A different type throws the subtree away. The same type keeps state. Lists match by key. Index keys suit static lists only.
rows: throws away the subtree, state too
keeps the instance and its state
fine only if the list never reorders

scenes.title: Why does one click add only 1?
scenes.statement: A button calls setCount(count + 1) three times. You expect +3. The screen shows 1. Explain it and fix it.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, count is zero, and one click calls set count three times. We want three, but the screen shows one.

scenes.head: What a state change does
scenes.say: First, what React actually does. A state change schedules a render. React runs your component again, and its children by default. It compares the new tree to the old one. Then it patches only the differences into the real page.

scenes.head: Think of photographs
scenes.say: Think of photographs. Each time your component renders, React takes a photo of your screen. In this photo, count is zero, frozen. A click asks for a new photo, where count is one. You never edit an old photo.

scenes.head: Three calls, one photo
scenes.say: In this render, count is zero. So all three calls say zero plus one. The screen ends at one, not three. And set state does not change count right now, it only schedules a render. Fix it with an updater function: each call gets the latest value. Now you get three.
Your turn. Count is zero. One click calls set count of count plus one, then set count with an updater, c becomes c plus one. What does the screen show? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The update queue, in order
scenes.say: Two. React queues both calls and applies them in order. State starts at zero. The first call sets it to one. The updater receives that one, and returns two. React renders once, with two.

scenes.title: Why does the timer stick at 1?
scenes.statement: A counter starts an interval that adds one every second. It shows 1, then never moves again.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, an interval that calls set count of count plus one every second. We want one, two, three. We get one, forever.

scenes.head: A sticky note for React
scenes.say: Think of a sticky note you hand to React. After you paint the screen, do this. Redo it only if a listed value changed. And the note has a second part: how to undo it first. That is an effect, its dependency list, and its cleanup.

scenes.head: Dependencies and cleanup
scenes.say: The first effect sets the page title. Its list holds count, so it re-runs when count changes. The second starts a timer, and returns a cleanup that stops it. React runs the cleanup before the next effect, and when the component leaves. Empty list: run once, after the first render. No list: after every render.

scenes.head: Why the interval is stale
scenes.say: Here is the bug. In render one, count is zero. The effect runs once, and its callback captures that zero. Every second the callback sets zero plus one. State becomes one. Render two has count one, but the effect never re-runs. The old callback still holds zero, so it sets one again.
Your turn. Keep the empty list, but write the updater: set count of c becomes c plus one. The interval ticks once a second. What does the screen show after five seconds? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Interval uses `setCount(c => c + 1)`, deps `[]`. After 5 s?

scenes.head: Two ways to fix it
scenes.say: Five. The updater never reads count, so there is nothing stale to capture. It always receives the latest value. The other fix is to list count in the dependency list. Then the effect re-runs each render, with a fresh callback. Never delete count from the list just to quiet it.

scenes.head: Hooks follow-ups
scenes.say: Follow-ups. Rules of hooks? Top level only, never in loops or conditions. An effect with no list? It runs after every render. Why must the list be honest? A missing value is a stale closure. Is set state synchronous? No, it schedules a render.
rows: top level only: no loops, no conditions

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is the virtual D O M? A cheap tree React diffs, then patches the real page. Why do keys matter? They give list items identity. Index as key? Only for static lists. Random keys? They remount every row. Common mistake: index keys with inputs.
rows: a cheap tree React diffs, then patches the page
identity for list items: stable ids
index: static lists only. random: remounts every row
index keys on rows with inputs or state

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does use state work? Each render is a snapshot. What is a stale closure? A callback that captured an old value. Fix it with the updater or an honest dependency list. Effect with no array? Every render.
rows: each render is a snapshot; updater for old-to-new
a callback that captured an old value
updater, or an honest dependency list

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Do these next. Build a todo list, break it with index keys, then fix it. Write an interval counter, and fix the stuck one both ways. Turn on the exhaustive deps lint rule.
rows: Todo list with inputs: break it with `key={i}`, fix it
Interval counter: reproduce the stuck 1, fix it two ways

scenes.say: So say this. React re-runs the component, diffs the trees, and patches only what changed. Keys are identity, so use stable ids. And each render is a snapshot, so use the updater, and keep effect dependencies honest.

Keys are identity: use stable ids, not indexes.
Each render is a snapshot: updater + honest deps.
